# Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sets)

## Basic Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.sets)

   class sympy.sets.sets.Set(**args*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L47-L851)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set)

The base class for any kind of set.

Explanation

This is not meant to be used directly as a container of items. It does not behave like the builtin `set`; see [`FiniteSet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.FiniteSet) for that.

Real intervals are represented by the [`Interval`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Interval) class and unions of sets by the [`Union`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Union) class. The empty set is represented by the [`EmptySet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.EmptySet) class and available as a singleton as `S.EmptySet`.

   as_relational(*symbol*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L849-L851)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.as_relational)

Rewrites the set as a relational.

    property boundary[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.boundary)

The boundary or frontier of a set.

Explanation

A point x is on the boundary of a set S if

1. x is in the closure of S. I.e. Every neighborhood of x contains a point in S.
2. x is not in the interior of S. I.e. There does not exist an open set centered on x contained entirely within S.

There are the points on the outer rim of S. If S is open then these points need not actually be contained within S.

For example, the boundary of an interval is its start and end points. This is true regardless of whether or not the interval is open.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(0, 1).boundary
{0, 1}
>>> Interval(0, 1, True, False).boundary
{0, 1}
```

  Copy to clipboard          property closure[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.closure)

Property method which returns the closure of a set. The closure is defined as the union of the set itself and its boundary.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import S, Interval
>>> S.Reals.closure
Reals
>>> Interval(0, 1).closure
Interval(0, 1)
```

  Copy to clipboard          complement(*universe*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L219-L234)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.complement)

The complement of ‘self’ w.r.t the given universe.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, S
>>> Interval(0, 1).complement(S.Reals)
Union(Interval.open(-oo, 0), Interval.open(1, oo))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(0, 1).complement(S.UniversalSet)
Complement(UniversalSet, Interval(0, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard          contains(*other*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L341-L387)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.contains)

Returns a SymPy value indicating whether `other` is contained in `self`: `true` if it is, `false` if it is not, else an unevaluated `Contains` expression (or, as in the case of ConditionSet and a union of FiniteSet/Intervals, an expression indicating the conditions for containment).

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, S
>>> from sympy.abc import x
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(0, 1).contains(0.5)
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

As a shortcut it is possible to use the `in` operator, but that will raise an error unless an affirmative true or false is not obtained.

```
>>> Interval(0, 1).contains(x)
(0 <= x) & (x <= 1)
>>> x in Interval(0, 1)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
TypeError: did not evaluate to a bool: None
```

  Copy to clipboard

The result of ‘in’ is a bool, not a SymPy value

```
>>> 1 in Interval(0, 2)
True
>>> _ is S.true
False
```

  Copy to clipboard          property inf[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.inf)

The infimum of `self`.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, Union
>>> Interval(0, 1).inf
0
>>> Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3)).inf
0
```

  Copy to clipboard          property interior[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.interior)

Property method which returns the interior of a set. The interior of a set S consists all points of S that do not belong to the boundary of S.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(0, 1).interior
Interval.open(0, 1)
>>> Interval(0, 1).boundary.interior
EmptySet
```

  Copy to clipboard          intersect(*other*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L166-L185)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.intersect)

Returns the intersection of ‘self’ and ‘other’.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(1, 3).intersect(Interval(1, 2))
Interval(1, 2)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> from sympy import imageset, Lambda, symbols, S
>>> n, m = symbols('n m')
>>> a = imageset(Lambda(n, 2*n), S.Integers)
>>> a.intersect(imageset(Lambda(m, 2*m + 1), S.Integers))
EmptySet
```

  Copy to clipboard          intersection(*other*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L187-L191)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.intersection)

Alias for [`intersect()`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.intersect)

    property is_closed[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.is_closed)

A property method to check whether a set is closed.

Explanation

A set is closed if its complement is an open set. The closedness of a subset of the reals is determined with respect to R and its standard topology.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(0, 1).is_closed
True
```

  Copy to clipboard          is_disjoint(*other*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L193-L211)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.is_disjoint)

Returns True if `self` and `other` are disjoint.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(0, 2).is_disjoint(Interval(1, 2))
False
>>> Interval(0, 2).is_disjoint(Interval(3, 4))
True
```

      property is_open[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.is_open)

Property method to check whether a set is open.

Explanation

A set is open if and only if it has an empty intersection with its boundary. In particular, a subset A of the reals is open if and only if each one of its points is contained in an open interval that is a subset of A.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import S
>>> S.Reals.is_open
True
>>> S.Rationals.is_open
False
```

    property kind[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.kind)

The kind of a Set

Explanation

Any [`Set`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set) will have kind [`SetKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.conditionset.SetKind) which is parametrised by the kind of the elements of the set. For example most sets are sets of numbers and will have kind `SetKind(NumberKind)`. If elements of sets are different in kind than their kind will `SetKind(UndefinedKind)`. See [`sympy.core.kind.Kind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/core.html#sympy.core.kind.Kind) for an explanation of the kind system.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, Matrix, FiniteSet, EmptySet, ProductSet, PowerSet
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> FiniteSet(Matrix([1, 2])).kind
SetKind(MatrixKind(NumberKind))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(1, 2).kind
SetKind(NumberKind)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> EmptySet.kind
SetKind()
```

  Copy to clipboard

A [`sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet) is a set of sets:

```
>>> PowerSet({1, 2, 3}).kind
SetKind(SetKind(NumberKind))
```

  Copy to clipboard

A [`ProductSet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet) represents the set of tuples of elements of other sets. Its kind is [`sympy.core.containers.TupleKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/core.html#sympy.core.containers.TupleKind) parametrised by the kinds of the elements of those sets:

```
>>> p = ProductSet(FiniteSet(1, 2), FiniteSet(3, 4))
>>> list(p)
[(1, 3), (2, 3), (1, 4), (2, 4)]
>>> p.kind
SetKind(TupleKind(NumberKind, NumberKind))
```

  Copy to clipboard

When all elements of the set do not have same kind, the kind will be returned as `SetKind(UndefinedKind)`:

```
>>> FiniteSet(0, Matrix([1, 2])).kind
SetKind(UndefinedKind)
```

  Copy to clipboard

The kind of the elements of a set are given by the `element_kind` attribute of `SetKind`:

```
>>> Interval(1, 2).kind.element_kind
NumberKind
```

  Copy to clipboard

      union(*other*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L139-L164)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.union)

Returns the union of `self` and `other`.

Examples

As a shortcut it is possible to use the `+` operator:

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, FiniteSet
>>> Interval(0, 1).union(Interval(2, 3))
Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3))
>>> Interval(0, 1) + Interval(2, 3)
Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3))
>>> Interval(1, 2, True, True) + FiniteSet(2, 3)
Union({3}, Interval.Lopen(1, 2))
```

  Copy to clipboard

Similarly it is possible to use the `-` operator for set differences:

```
>>> Interval(0, 2) - Interval(0, 1)
Interval.Lopen(1, 2)
>>> Interval(1, 3) - FiniteSet(2)
Union(Interval.Ropen(1, 2), Interval.Lopen(2, 3))
```

  Copy to clipboard           sympy.sets.sets.imageset(**args*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L2442-L2567)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.imageset)

Return an image of the set under transformation `f`.

Explanation

If this function cannot compute the image, it returns an unevaluated ImageSet object.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import S, Interval, imageset, sin, Lambda
>>> from sympy.abc import x
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(x, 2*x, Interval(0, 2))
Interval(0, 4)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(lambda x: 2*x, Interval(0, 2))
Interval(0, 4)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(Lambda(x, sin(x)), Interval(-2, 1))
ImageSet(Lambda(x, sin(x)), Interval(-2, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(sin, Interval(-2, 1))
ImageSet(Lambda(x, sin(x)), Interval(-2, 1))
>>> imageset(lambda y: x + y, Interval(-2, 1))
ImageSet(Lambda(y, x + y), Interval(-2, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard

Expressions applied to the set of Integers are simplified to show as few negatives as possible and linear expressions are converted to a canonical form. If this is not desirable then the unevaluated ImageSet should be used.

```
>>> imageset(x, -2*x + 5, S.Integers)
ImageSet(Lambda(x, 2*x + 1), Integers)
```

  Copy to clipboard

## Elementary Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#elementary-sets)

   class sympy.sets.sets.Interval(  *start*, *end*, *left_open=False*, *right_open=False*,  )[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L1035-L1316)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Interval)

Represents a real interval as a Set.

  Usage:

Returns an interval with end points `start` and `end`.

For `left_open=True` (default `left_open` is `False`) the interval will be open on the left. Similarly, for `right_open=True` the interval will be open on the right.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, Interval
>>> Interval(0, 1)
Interval(0, 1)
>>> Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
>>> Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
>>> Interval.Lopen(0, 1)
Interval.Lopen(0, 1)
>>> Interval.open(0, 1)
Interval.open(0, 1)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> a = Symbol('a', real=True)
>>> Interval(0, a)
Interval(0, a)
```

  Copy to clipboard

Notes

- Only real end points are supported
- `Interval(a, b)` with 𝑎 >𝑏 will return the empty set
- Use the `evalf()` method to turn an Interval into an mpmath `mpi` interval instance

References

   [[R1182](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#id4)]

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_%28mathematics%29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_%28mathematics%29)

## Compound Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#compound-sets)

   class sympy.sets.sets.Union(**args*, ***kwargs*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L1319-L1506)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Union)

Represents a union of sets as a [`Set`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set).

  Parameters:

**args** : iterable[Set]

>
> The input sets to be united.
>

**evaluate** : bool, optional

>
> If True (default from sympy.core.parameters.global_parameters.evaluate),
> the constructor simplifies the union.
>

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Union, Interval
>>> Union(Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4))
Union(Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4))
```

  Copy to clipboard

The Union constructor will always try to merge overlapping intervals, if possible. For example:

```
>>> Union(Interval(1, 2), Interval(2, 3))
Interval(1, 3)
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`Intersection`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Intersection)

     class sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet(**sets*, ***assumptions*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L854-L1032)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet)

Represents a Cartesian Product of Sets.

Explanation

Returns a Cartesian product given several sets as either an iterable or individual arguments.

Can use `*` operator on any sets for convenient shorthand.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, FiniteSet, ProductSet
>>> I = Interval(0, 5); S = FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)
>>> ProductSet(I, S)
ProductSet(Interval(0, 5), {1, 2, 3})
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> (2, 2) in ProductSet(I, S)
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(0, 1) * Interval(0, 1) # The unit square
ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval(0, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> coin = FiniteSet('H', 'T')
>>> set(coin**2)
{(H, H), (H, T), (T, H), (T, T)}
```

  Copy to clipboard

The Cartesian product is not commutative or associative e.g.:

```
>>> I*S == S*I
False
>>> (I*I)*I == I*(I*I)
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

Notes

- Passes most operations down to the argument sets

References

   [[R1186](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#id8)]

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product)

     property is_iterable[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet.is_iterable)

A property method which tests whether a set is iterable or not. Returns True if set is iterable, otherwise returns False.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import FiniteSet, Interval
>>> I = Interval(0, 1)
>>> A = FiniteSet(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
>>> I.is_iterable
False
>>> A.is_iterable
True
```

Represents the disjoint union (also known as the external disjoint union) of a finite number of sets.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import DisjointUnion, FiniteSet, Interval, Union, Symbol
>>> A = FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)
>>> B = Interval(0, 5)
>>> DisjointUnion(A, B)

>>> DisjointUnion(A, B).rewrite(Union)

>>> C = FiniteSet(Symbol('x'), Symbol('y'), Symbol('z'))
>>> DisjointUnion(C, C)
DisjointUnion({x, y, z}, {x, y, z})
>>> DisjointUnion(C, C).rewrite(Union)
ProductSet({x, y, z}, {0, 1})

     class sympy.sets.fancysets.ImageSet(*flambda*, **sets*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L292-L517)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ImageSet)

Image of a set under a mathematical function. The transformation must be given as a Lambda function which has as many arguments as the elements of the set upon which it operates, e.g. 1 argument when acting on the set of integers or 2 arguments when acting on a complex region.

This function is not normally called directly, but is called from `imageset`.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, S, pi, Dummy, Lambda
>>> from sympy import FiniteSet, ImageSet, Interval
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> x = Symbol('x')
>>> N = S.Naturals
>>> squares = ImageSet(Lambda(x, x**2), N) # {x**2 for x in N}
>>> 4 in squares
True
>>> 5 in squares
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> FiniteSet(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10).intersect(squares)
{1, 4, 9}
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> square_iterable = iter(squares)
>>> for i in range(4):
...     next(square_iterable)
1
4
9
16
```

  Copy to clipboard

If you want to get value for 𝑥 = 2, 1/2 etc. (Please check whether the 𝑥 value is in `base_set` or not before passing it as args)

```
>>> squares.lamda(2)
4
>>> squares.lamda(S(1)/2)
1/4
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> n = Dummy('n')
>>> solutions = ImageSet(Lambda(n, n*pi), S.Integers) # solutions of sin(x) = 0
>>> dom = Interval(-1, 1)
>>> dom.intersect(solutions)
{0}
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`sympy.sets.sets.imageset`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.imageset)

     class sympy.sets.fancysets.Range(**args*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L520-L1021)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.Range)

Represents a range of integers. Can be called as `Range(stop)`, `Range(start, stop)`, or `Range(start, stop, step)`; when `step` is not given it defaults to 1.

`Range(stop)` is the same as `Range(0, stop, 1)` and the stop value (just as for Python ranges) is not included in the Range values.

```
>>> from sympy import Range
>>> list(Range(3))
[0, 1, 2]
```

  Copy to clipboard

The step can also be negative:

```
>>> list(Range(10, 0, -2))
[10, 8, 6, 4, 2]
```

  Copy to clipboard

The stop value is made canonical so equivalent ranges always have the same args:

```
>>> Range(0, 10, 3)
Range(0, 12, 3)
```

  Copy to clipboard

Infinite ranges are allowed. `oo` and `-oo` are never included in the set (`Range` is always a subset of `Integers`). If the starting point is infinite, then the final value is `stop - step`. To iterate such a range, it needs to be reversed:

```
>>> from sympy import oo
>>> r = Range(-oo, 1)
>>> r[-1]
0
>>> next(iter(r))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
TypeError: Cannot iterate over Range with infinite start
>>> next(iter(r.reversed))
0
```

  Copy to clipboard

Although `Range` is a `Set` (and supports the normal set operations) it maintains the order of the elements and can be used in contexts where `range` would be used.

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Range(0, 10, 2).intersect(Interval(3, 7))
Range(4, 8, 2)
>>> list(_)
[4, 6]
```

  Copy to clipboard

Although slicing of a Range will always return a Range – possibly empty – an empty set will be returned from any intersection that is empty:

```
>>> Range(3)[:0]
Range(0, 0, 1)
>>> Range(3).intersect(Interval(4, oo))
EmptySet
>>> Range(3).intersect(Range(4, oo))
EmptySet
```

  Copy to clipboard

Range will accept symbolic arguments but has very limited support for doing anything other than displaying the Range:

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, pprint
>>> from sympy.abc import i, j, k
>>> Range(i, j, k).start
i
>>> Range(i, j, k).inf
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: invalid method for symbolic range
```

  Copy to clipboard

Better success will be had when using integer symbols:

```
>>> n = Symbol('n', integer=True)
>>> r = Range(n, n + 20, 3)
>>> r.inf
n
>>> pprint(r)
{n, n + 3, ..., n + 18}
```

  Copy to clipboard           class sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion(*sets*, *polar=False*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L1111-L1384)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion)

Represents the Set of all Complex Numbers. It can represent a region of Complex Plane in both the standard forms Polar and Rectangular coordinates.

- Polar Form Input is in the form of the ProductSet or Union of ProductSets of the intervals of `r` and `theta`, and use the flag `polar=True`.   𝑍={𝑧∈ℂ∣𝑧=𝑟×(cos⁡(𝜃)+𝐼⁢sin⁡(𝜃)),𝑟∈[𝚛],𝜃∈[𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚝𝚊]}
- Rectangular Form Input is in the form of the ProductSet or Union of ProductSets of interval of x and y, the real and imaginary parts of the Complex numbers in a plane. Default input type is in rectangular form.
   𝑍={𝑧∈ℂ∣𝑧=𝑥+𝐼⁢𝑦,𝑥∈[re⁡(𝑧)],𝑦∈[im⁡(𝑧)]}

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import ComplexRegion, Interval, S, I, Union
>>> a = Interval(2, 3)
>>> b = Interval(4, 6)
>>> c1 = ComplexRegion(a*b)  # Rectangular Form
>>> c1
CartesianComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 6)))
```

  Copy to clipboard
- c1 represents the rectangular region in complex plane surrounded by the coordinates (2, 4), (3, 4), (3, 6) and (2, 6), of the four vertices.

```
>>> c = Interval(1, 8)
>>> c2 = ComplexRegion(Union(a*b, b*c))
>>> c2
CartesianComplexRegion(Union(ProductSet(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 6)), ProductSet(Interval(4, 6), Interval(1, 8))))
```

  Copy to clipboard
- c2 represents the Union of two rectangular regions in complex plane. One of them surrounded by the coordinates of c1 and other surrounded by the coordinates (4, 1), (6, 1), (6, 8) and (4, 8).

```
>>> 2.5 + 4.5*I in c1
True
>>> 2.5 + 6.5*I in c1
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> r = Interval(0, 1)
>>> theta = Interval(0, 2*S.Pi)
>>> c2 = ComplexRegion(r*theta, polar=True)  # Polar Form
>>> c2  # unit Disk
PolarComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval.Ropen(0, 2*pi)))
```

  Copy to clipboard
- c2 represents the region in complex plane inside the Unit Disk centered at the origin.

```
>>> 0.5 + 0.5*I in c2
True
>>> 1 + 2*I in c2
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> unit_disk = ComplexRegion(Interval(0, 1)*Interval(0, 2*S.Pi), polar=True)
>>> upper_half_unit_disk = ComplexRegion(Interval(0, 1)*Interval(0, S.Pi), polar=True)
>>> intersection = unit_disk.intersect(upper_half_unit_disk)
>>> intersection
PolarComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval(0, pi)))
>>> intersection == upper_half_unit_disk
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`CartesianComplexRegion`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.CartesianComplexRegion), [`PolarComplexRegion`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.PolarComplexRegion), [`Complexes`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.Complexes)

    property a_interval[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion.a_interval)

Return the union of intervals of 𝑥 when, self is in rectangular form, or the union of intervals of 𝑟 when self is in polar form.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, ComplexRegion, Union
>>> a = Interval(2, 3)
>>> b = Interval(4, 5)
>>> c = Interval(1, 7)
>>> C1 = ComplexRegion(a*b)
>>> C1.a_interval
Interval(2, 3)
>>> C2 = ComplexRegion(Union(a*b, b*c))
>>> C2.a_interval
Union(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 5))
```

  Copy to clipboard          property b_interval[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion.b_interval)

Return the union of intervals of 𝑦 when, self is in rectangular form, or the union of intervals of 𝑡⁢ℎ⁡𝑒⁢𝑡⁢𝑎 when self is in polar form.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, ComplexRegion, Union
>>> a = Interval(2, 3)
>>> b = Interval(4, 5)
>>> c = Interval(1, 7)
>>> C1 = ComplexRegion(a*b)
>>> C1.b_interval
Interval(4, 5)
>>> C2 = ComplexRegion(Union(a*b, b*c))
>>> C2.b_interval

Normalize a Real Set 𝑡⁢ℎ⁡𝑒⁢𝑡⁢𝑎 in the interval [0,2⁢𝜋). It returns a normalized value of theta in the Set. For Interval, a maximum of one cycle [0,2⁢𝜋], is returned i.e. for theta equal to [0,10⁢𝜋], returned normalized value would be [0,2⁢𝜋).   Raises:

## Power sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.powerset)

   class sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet(*arg*, *evaluate=None*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/powerset.py#L12-L128)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet)

A symbolic object representing a power set.

  Parameters:

**arg** : Set

>
> The set to take power of.
>

**evaluate** : bool

>
> The flag to control evaluation.
> If the evaluation is disabled for finite sets, it can take
> advantage of using subset test as a membership test.
>

Notes

Power set P⁡(𝑆) is defined as a set containing all the subsets of 𝑆.

If the set 𝑆 is a finite set, its power set would have 2|𝑆| elements, where |𝑆| denotes the cardinality of 𝑆.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import PowerSet, S, FiniteSet
```

  Copy to clipboard

A power set of a finite set:

```
>>> PowerSet(FiniteSet(1, 2, 3))
PowerSet({1, 2, 3})
```

  Copy to clipboard

A power set of an empty set:

```
>>> PowerSet(S.EmptySet)
PowerSet(EmptySet)
>>> PowerSet(PowerSet(S.EmptySet))
PowerSet(PowerSet(EmptySet))
```

  Copy to clipboard

A power set of an infinite set:

```
>>> PowerSet(S.Reals)
PowerSet(Reals)
```

  Copy to clipboard

Evaluating the power set of a finite set to its explicit form:

```
>>> PowerSet(FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)).rewrite(FiniteSet)
FiniteSet(EmptySet, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {1, 2, 3})
```

  Copy to clipboard

## Condition Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.conditionset)

   class sympy.sets.conditionset.ConditionSet(  *sym*, *condition*, *base_set=UniversalSet*,  )[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/conditionset.py#L20-L247)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.conditionset.ConditionSet)

Set of elements which satisfies a given condition.

   {𝑥∣condition⁡(𝑥)=𝚃𝚛𝚞𝚎,𝑥∈𝑆}

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, S, ConditionSet, pi, Eq, sin, Interval
>>> from sympy.abc import x, y, z
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> sin_sols = ConditionSet(x, Eq(sin(x), 0), Interval(0, 2*pi))
>>> 2*pi in sin_sols
True
>>> pi/2 in sin_sols
False
>>> 3*pi in sin_sols
False
>>> 5 in ConditionSet(x, x**2 > 4, S.Reals)
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

If the value is not in the base set, the result is false:

```
>>> 5 in ConditionSet(x, x**2 > 4, Interval(2, 4))
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

Notes

Symbols with assumptions should be avoided or else the condition may evaluate without consideration of the set:

```
>>> n = Symbol('n', negative=True)
>>> cond = (n > 0); cond
False
>>> ConditionSet(n, cond, S.Integers)
EmptySet
```

  Copy to clipboard

Only free symbols can be changed by using 𝑠⁢𝑢⁢𝑏⁢𝑠:

```
>>> c = ConditionSet(x, x < 1, {x, z})
>>> c.subs(x, y)
ConditionSet(x, x < 1, {y, z})
```

  Copy to clipboard

To check if `pi` is in `c` use:

```
>>> pi in c
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

If no base set is specified, the universal set is implied:

```
>>> ConditionSet(x, x < 1).base_set
UniversalSet
```

  Copy to clipboard

Only symbols or symbol-like expressions can be used:

```
>>> ConditionSet(x + 1, x + 1 < 1, S.Integers)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: non-symbol dummy not recognized in condition
```

  Copy to clipboard

When the base set is a ConditionSet, the symbols will be unified if possible with preference for the outermost symbols:

```
>>> ConditionSet(x, x < y, ConditionSet(z, z + y < 2, S.Integers))
ConditionSet(x, (x < y) & (x + y < 2), Integers)
```

   class sympy.sets.conditionset.SetKind(*element_kind=None*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L2785-L2830)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.conditionset.SetKind)

SetKind is kind for all Sets

Every instance of Set will have kind `SetKind` parametrised by the kind of the elements of the `Set`. The kind of the elements might be `NumberKind`, or `TupleKind` or something else. When not all elements have the same kind then the kind of the elements will be given as `UndefinedKind`.

>

> will have the same kind. Otherwise the kind should
> sympy.core.kind.UndefinedKind. The element_kind argument is optional but
> should only be omitted in the case of EmptySet whose kind is simply
> SetKind()
>

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(1, 2).kind
SetKind(NumberKind)
>>> Interval(1,2).kind.element_kind
NumberKind
```

## Iteration over sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#iteration-over-sets)

For set unions, {𝑎,𝑏} ∪{𝑥,𝑦} can be treated as {𝑎,𝑏,𝑥,𝑦} for iteration regardless of the distinctiveness of the elements, however, for set intersections, assuming that {𝑎,𝑏} ∩{𝑥,𝑦} is ∅ or {𝑎,𝑏} would not always be valid, since some of 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑥 or 𝑦 may or may not be the elements of the intersection.

Iterating over the elements of a set involving intersection, complement, or symmetric difference yields (possibly duplicate) elements of the set provided that all elements are known to be the elements of the set. If any element cannot be determined to be a member of a set then the iteration gives `TypeError`. This happens in the same cases where `x in y` would give an error.

There are some reasons to implement like this, even if it breaks the consistency with how the python set iterator works. We keep in mind that sympy set comprehension like `FiniteSet(*s)` from a existing sympy sets could be a common usage. And this approach would make `FiniteSet(*s)` to be consistent with any symbolic set processing methods like `FiniteSet(*simplify(s))`.

class sympy.sets.sets.Set(**args*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L47-L851)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set)

The base class for any kind of set.

Explanation

This is not meant to be used directly as a container of items. It does not behave like the builtin `set`; see [`FiniteSet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.FiniteSet) for that.

Real intervals are represented by the [`Interval`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Interval) class and unions of sets by the [`Union`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Union) class. The empty set is represented by the [`EmptySet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.EmptySet) class and available as a singleton as `S.EmptySet`.

   as_relational(*symbol*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L849-L851)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.as_relational)

Rewrites the set as a relational.

    property boundary[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.boundary)

The boundary or frontier of a set.

Explanation

A point x is on the boundary of a set S if

1. x is in the closure of S. I.e. Every neighborhood of x contains a point in S.
2. x is not in the interior of S. I.e. There does not exist an open set centered on x contained entirely within S.

There are the points on the outer rim of S. If S is open then these points need not actually be contained within S.

For example, the boundary of an interval is its start and end points. This is true regardless of whether or not the interval is open.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(0, 1).boundary
{0, 1}
>>> Interval(0, 1, True, False).boundary
{0, 1}
```

    property kind[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.kind)

The kind of a Set

Explanation

Any [`Set`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set) will have kind [`SetKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.conditionset.SetKind) which is parametrised by the kind of the elements of the set. For example most sets are sets of numbers and will have kind `SetKind(NumberKind)`. If elements of sets are different in kind than their kind will `SetKind(UndefinedKind)`. See [`sympy.core.kind.Kind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/core.html#sympy.core.kind.Kind) for an explanation of the kind system.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, Matrix, FiniteSet, EmptySet, ProductSet, PowerSet
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> FiniteSet(Matrix([1, 2])).kind
SetKind(MatrixKind(NumberKind))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(1, 2).kind
SetKind(NumberKind)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> EmptySet.kind
SetKind()
```

  Copy to clipboard

A [`sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet) is a set of sets:

```
>>> PowerSet({1, 2, 3}).kind
SetKind(SetKind(NumberKind))
```

  Copy to clipboard

A [`ProductSet`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet) represents the set of tuples of elements of other sets. Its kind is [`sympy.core.containers.TupleKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/core.html#sympy.core.containers.TupleKind) parametrised by the kinds of the elements of those sets:

```
>>> p = ProductSet(FiniteSet(1, 2), FiniteSet(3, 4))
>>> list(p)
[(1, 3), (2, 3), (1, 4), (2, 4)]
>>> p.kind
SetKind(TupleKind(NumberKind, NumberKind))
```

  Copy to clipboard

When all elements of the set do not have same kind, the kind will be returned as `SetKind(UndefinedKind)`:

```
>>> FiniteSet(0, Matrix([1, 2])).kind
SetKind(UndefinedKind)
```

  Copy to clipboard

The kind of the elements of a set are given by the `element_kind` attribute of `SetKind`:

```
>>> Interval(1, 2).kind.element_kind
NumberKind
```

  Copy to clipboard

      union(*other*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L139-L164)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set.union)

Returns the union of `self` and `other`.

Examples

As a shortcut it is possible to use the `+` operator:

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, FiniteSet
>>> Interval(0, 1).union(Interval(2, 3))
Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3))
>>> Interval(0, 1) + Interval(2, 3)
Union(Interval(0, 1), Interval(2, 3))
>>> Interval(1, 2, True, True) + FiniteSet(2, 3)
Union({3}, Interval.Lopen(1, 2))
```

  Copy to clipboard

Similarly it is possible to use the `-` operator for set differences:

```
>>> Interval(0, 2) - Interval(0, 1)
Interval.Lopen(1, 2)
>>> Interval(1, 3) - FiniteSet(2)
Union(Interval.Ropen(1, 2), Interval.Lopen(2, 3))
```

  Copy to clipboard           sympy.sets.sets.imageset(**args*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L2442-L2567)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.imageset)

Return an image of the set under transformation `f`.

Explanation

If this function cannot compute the image, it returns an unevaluated ImageSet object.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import S, Interval, imageset, sin, Lambda
>>> from sympy.abc import x
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(x, 2*x, Interval(0, 2))
Interval(0, 4)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(lambda x: 2*x, Interval(0, 2))
Interval(0, 4)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(Lambda(x, sin(x)), Interval(-2, 1))
ImageSet(Lambda(x, sin(x)), Interval(-2, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> imageset(sin, Interval(-2, 1))
ImageSet(Lambda(x, sin(x)), Interval(-2, 1))
>>> imageset(lambda y: x + y, Interval(-2, 1))
ImageSet(Lambda(y, x + y), Interval(-2, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard

Expressions applied to the set of Integers are simplified to show as few negatives as possible and linear expressions are converted to a canonical form. If this is not desirable then the unevaluated ImageSet should be used.

```
>>> imageset(x, -2*x + 5, S.Integers)
ImageSet(Lambda(x, 2*x + 1), Integers)
```

  Copy to clipboard

# Elementary Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#elementary-sets)

class sympy.sets.sets.Interval(  *start*, *end*, *left_open=False*, *right_open=False*,  )[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L1035-L1316)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Interval)

Represents a real interval as a Set.

  Usage:

Returns an interval with end points `start` and `end`.

For `left_open=True` (default `left_open` is `False`) the interval will be open on the left. Similarly, for `right_open=True` the interval will be open on the right.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, Interval
>>> Interval(0, 1)
Interval(0, 1)
>>> Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
>>> Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
Interval.Ropen(0, 1)
>>> Interval.Lopen(0, 1)
Interval.Lopen(0, 1)
>>> Interval.open(0, 1)
Interval.open(0, 1)
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> a = Symbol('a', real=True)
>>> Interval(0, a)
Interval(0, a)
```

  Copy to clipboard

Notes

- Only real end points are supported
- `Interval(a, b)` with 𝑎 >𝑏 will return the empty set
- Use the `evalf()` method to turn an Interval into an mpmath `mpi` interval instance

References

   [[R1182](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#id4)]

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_%28mathematics%29](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_%28mathematics%29)

class sympy.sets.sets.Union(**args*, ***kwargs*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L1319-L1506)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Union)

Represents a union of sets as a [`Set`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Set).

  Parameters:

**args** : iterable[Set]

>
> The input sets to be united.
>

**evaluate** : bool, optional

>
> If True (default from sympy.core.parameters.global_parameters.evaluate),
> the constructor simplifies the union.
>

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Union, Interval
>>> Union(Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4))
Union(Interval(1, 2), Interval(3, 4))
```

  Copy to clipboard

The Union constructor will always try to merge overlapping intervals, if possible. For example:

```
>>> Union(Interval(1, 2), Interval(2, 3))
Interval(1, 3)
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`Intersection`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.Intersection)

     class sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet(**sets*, ***assumptions*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L854-L1032)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet)

Represents a Cartesian Product of Sets.

Explanation

Returns a Cartesian product given several sets as either an iterable or individual arguments.

Can use `*` operator on any sets for convenient shorthand.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, FiniteSet, ProductSet
>>> I = Interval(0, 5); S = FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)
>>> ProductSet(I, S)
ProductSet(Interval(0, 5), {1, 2, 3})
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> (2, 2) in ProductSet(I, S)
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> Interval(0, 1) * Interval(0, 1) # The unit square
ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval(0, 1))
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> coin = FiniteSet('H', 'T')
>>> set(coin**2)
{(H, H), (H, T), (T, H), (T, T)}
```

  Copy to clipboard

The Cartesian product is not commutative or associative e.g.:

```
>>> I*S == S*I
False
>>> (I*I)*I == I*(I*I)
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

Notes

- Passes most operations down to the argument sets

References

   [[R1186](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#id8)]

[https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartesian_product)

     property is_iterable[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.ProductSet.is_iterable)

     class sympy.sets.sets.DisjointUnion(**sets*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L2287-L2439)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.DisjointUnion)

Represents the disjoint union (also known as the external disjoint union) of a finite number of sets.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import DisjointUnion, FiniteSet, Interval, Union, Symbol
>>> A = FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)
>>> B = Interval(0, 5)
>>> DisjointUnion(A, B)
DisjointUnion({1, 2, 3}, Interval(0, 5))
>>> DisjointUnion(A, B).rewrite(Union)
Union(ProductSet({1, 2, 3}, {0}), ProductSet(Interval(0, 5), {1}))
>>> C = FiniteSet(Symbol('x'), Symbol('y'), Symbol('z'))
>>> DisjointUnion(C, C)
DisjointUnion({x, y, z}, {x, y, z})
>>> DisjointUnion(C, C).rewrite(Union)
ProductSet({x, y, z}, {0, 1})
```

     class sympy.sets.fancysets.ImageSet(*flambda*, **sets*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L292-L517)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ImageSet)

Image of a set under a mathematical function. The transformation must be given as a Lambda function which has as many arguments as the elements of the set upon which it operates, e.g. 1 argument when acting on the set of integers or 2 arguments when acting on a complex region.

This function is not normally called directly, but is called from `imageset`.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, S, pi, Dummy, Lambda
>>> from sympy import FiniteSet, ImageSet, Interval
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> x = Symbol('x')
>>> N = S.Naturals
>>> squares = ImageSet(Lambda(x, x**2), N) # {x**2 for x in N}
>>> 4 in squares
True
>>> 5 in squares
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> FiniteSet(0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10).intersect(squares)
{1, 4, 9}
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> square_iterable = iter(squares)
>>> for i in range(4):
...     next(square_iterable)
1
4
9
16
```

  Copy to clipboard

If you want to get value for 𝑥 = 2, 1/2 etc. (Please check whether the 𝑥 value is in `base_set` or not before passing it as args)

```
>>> squares.lamda(2)
4
>>> squares.lamda(S(1)/2)
1/4
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> n = Dummy('n')
>>> solutions = ImageSet(Lambda(n, n*pi), S.Integers) # solutions of sin(x) = 0
>>> dom = Interval(-1, 1)
>>> dom.intersect(solutions)
{0}
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`sympy.sets.sets.imageset`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.sets.imageset)

     class sympy.sets.fancysets.Range(**args*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L520-L1021)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.Range)

Represents a range of integers. Can be called as `Range(stop)`, `Range(start, stop)`, or `Range(start, stop, step)`; when `step` is not given it defaults to 1.

`Range(stop)` is the same as `Range(0, stop, 1)` and the stop value (just as for Python ranges) is not included in the Range values.

```
>>> from sympy import Range
>>> list(Range(3))
[0, 1, 2]
```

  Copy to clipboard

The step can also be negative:

```
>>> list(Range(10, 0, -2))
[10, 8, 6, 4, 2]
```

  Copy to clipboard

The stop value is made canonical so equivalent ranges always have the same args:

```
>>> Range(0, 10, 3)
Range(0, 12, 3)
```

  Copy to clipboard

Infinite ranges are allowed. `oo` and `-oo` are never included in the set (`Range` is always a subset of `Integers`). If the starting point is infinite, then the final value is `stop - step`. To iterate such a range, it needs to be reversed:

```
>>> from sympy import oo
>>> r = Range(-oo, 1)
>>> r[-1]
0
>>> next(iter(r))
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
TypeError: Cannot iterate over Range with infinite start
>>> next(iter(r.reversed))
0
```

  Copy to clipboard

Although `Range` is a `Set` (and supports the normal set operations) it maintains the order of the elements and can be used in contexts where `range` would be used.

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Range(0, 10, 2).intersect(Interval(3, 7))
Range(4, 8, 2)
>>> list(_)
[4, 6]
```

  Copy to clipboard

Although slicing of a Range will always return a Range – possibly empty – an empty set will be returned from any intersection that is empty:

```
>>> Range(3)[:0]
Range(0, 0, 1)
>>> Range(3).intersect(Interval(4, oo))
EmptySet
>>> Range(3).intersect(Range(4, oo))
EmptySet
```

  Copy to clipboard

Range will accept symbolic arguments but has very limited support for doing anything other than displaying the Range:

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, pprint
>>> from sympy.abc import i, j, k
>>> Range(i, j, k).start
i
>>> Range(i, j, k).inf
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: invalid method for symbolic range
```

  Copy to clipboard

Better success will be had when using integer symbols:

```
>>> n = Symbol('n', integer=True)
>>> r = Range(n, n + 20, 3)
>>> r.inf
n
>>> pprint(r)
{n, n + 3, ..., n + 18}
```

  Copy to clipboard           class sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion(*sets*, *polar=False*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L1111-L1384)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion)

Represents the Set of all Complex Numbers. It can represent a region of Complex Plane in both the standard forms Polar and Rectangular coordinates.

- Polar Form Input is in the form of the ProductSet or Union of ProductSets of the intervals of `r` and `theta`, and use the flag `polar=True`.   𝑍={𝑧∈ℂ∣𝑧=𝑟×(cos⁡(𝜃)+𝐼⁢sin⁡(𝜃)),𝑟∈[𝚛],𝜃∈[𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚝𝚊]}
- Rectangular Form Input is in the form of the ProductSet or Union of ProductSets of interval of x and y, the real and imaginary parts of the Complex numbers in a plane. Default input type is in rectangular form.
   𝑍={𝑧∈ℂ∣𝑧=𝑥+𝐼⁢𝑦,𝑥∈[re⁡(𝑧)],𝑦∈[im⁡(𝑧)]}

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import ComplexRegion, Interval, S, I, Union
>>> a = Interval(2, 3)
>>> b = Interval(4, 6)
>>> c1 = ComplexRegion(a*b)  # Rectangular Form
>>> c1
CartesianComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 6)))
```

  Copy to clipboard
- c1 represents the rectangular region in complex plane surrounded by the coordinates (2, 4), (3, 4), (3, 6) and (2, 6), of the four vertices.

```
>>> c = Interval(1, 8)
>>> c2 = ComplexRegion(Union(a*b, b*c))
>>> c2
CartesianComplexRegion(Union(ProductSet(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 6)), ProductSet(Interval(4, 6), Interval(1, 8))))
```

  Copy to clipboard
- c2 represents the Union of two rectangular regions in complex plane. One of them surrounded by the coordinates of c1 and other surrounded by the coordinates (4, 1), (6, 1), (6, 8) and (4, 8).

```
>>> 2.5 + 4.5*I in c1
True
>>> 2.5 + 6.5*I in c1
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> r = Interval(0, 1)
>>> theta = Interval(0, 2*S.Pi)
>>> c2 = ComplexRegion(r*theta, polar=True)  # Polar Form
>>> c2  # unit Disk
PolarComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval.Ropen(0, 2*pi)))
```

  Copy to clipboard
- c2 represents the region in complex plane inside the Unit Disk centered at the origin.

```
>>> 0.5 + 0.5*I in c2
True
>>> 1 + 2*I in c2
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> unit_disk = ComplexRegion(Interval(0, 1)*Interval(0, 2*S.Pi), polar=True)
>>> upper_half_unit_disk = ComplexRegion(Interval(0, 1)*Interval(0, S.Pi), polar=True)
>>> intersection = unit_disk.intersect(upper_half_unit_disk)
>>> intersection
PolarComplexRegion(ProductSet(Interval(0, 1), Interval(0, pi)))
>>> intersection == upper_half_unit_disk
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`CartesianComplexRegion`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.CartesianComplexRegion), [`PolarComplexRegion`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.PolarComplexRegion), [`Complexes`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.Complexes)

    property a_interval[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion.a_interval)

Return the union of intervals of 𝑥 when, self is in rectangular form, or the union of intervals of 𝑟 when self is in polar form.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, ComplexRegion, Union
>>> a = Interval(2, 3)
>>> b = Interval(4, 5)
>>> c = Interval(1, 7)
>>> C1 = ComplexRegion(a*b)
>>> C1.a_interval
Interval(2, 3)
>>> C2 = ComplexRegion(Union(a*b, b*c))
>>> C2.a_interval
Union(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 5))
```

  Copy to clipboard          property b_interval[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.ComplexRegion.b_interval)

Return the union of intervals of 𝑦 when, self is in rectangular form, or the union of intervals of 𝑡⁢ℎ⁡𝑒⁢𝑡⁢𝑎 when self is in polar form.

Examples

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval, ComplexRegion, Union
>>> a = Interval(2, 3)

Union(ProductSet(Interval(2, 3), Interval(4, 5)), ProductSet(Interval(4, 5), Interval(1, 7)))
```

     sympy.sets.fancysets.normalize_theta_set(*theta*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/fancysets.py#L1026-L1108)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.fancysets.normalize_theta_set)

Normalize a Real Set 𝑡⁢ℎ⁡𝑒⁢𝑡⁢𝑎 in the interval [0,2⁢𝜋). It returns a normalized value of theta in the Set. For Interval, a maximum of one cycle [0,2⁢𝜋], is returned i.e. for theta equal to [0,10⁢𝜋], returned normalized value would be [0,2⁢𝜋). As of now intervals with end points as non-multiples of `pi` is not supported.

  Raises:

**NotImplementedError**

>
> The algorithms for Normalizing theta Set are not yet
> implemented.
>

**ValueError**

>
> The input is not valid, i.e. the input is not a real set.
>

**RuntimeError**

>
> It is a bug, please report to the github issue tracker.
>

Examples

```
>>> from sympy.sets.fancysets import normalize_theta_set
>>> from sympy import Interval, FiniteSet, pi
>>> normalize_theta_set(Interval(9*pi/2, 5*pi))
Interval(pi/2, pi)
>>> normalize_theta_set(Interval(-3*pi/2, pi/2))
Interval.Ropen(0, 2*pi)
>>> normalize_theta_set(Interval(-pi/2, pi/2))
Union(Interval(0, pi/2), Interval.Ropen(3*pi/2, 2*pi))
>>> normalize_theta_set(Interval(-4*pi, 3*pi))
Interval.Ropen(0, 2*pi)
>>> normalize_theta_set(Interval(-3*pi/2, -pi/2))
Interval(pi/2, 3*pi/2)
>>> normalize_theta_set(FiniteSet(0, pi, 3*pi))
{0, pi}
```

Power sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.powerset)

# Power sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.powerset)

class sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet(*arg*, *evaluate=None*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/powerset.py#L12-L128)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.powerset.PowerSet)

A symbolic object representing a power set.

  Parameters:

**arg** : Set

>
> The set to take power of.
>

**evaluate** : bool

>
> The flag to control evaluation.
> If the evaluation is disabled for finite sets, it can take
> advantage of using subset test as a membership test.
>

Notes

Power set P⁡(𝑆) is defined as a set containing all the subsets of 𝑆.

If the set 𝑆 is a finite set, its power set would have 2|𝑆| elements, where |𝑆| denotes the cardinality of 𝑆.

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import PowerSet, S, FiniteSet
```

  Copy to clipboard

A power set of a finite set:

```
>>> PowerSet(FiniteSet(1, 2, 3))
PowerSet({1, 2, 3})
```

  Copy to clipboard

A power set of an empty set:

```
>>> PowerSet(S.EmptySet)
PowerSet(EmptySet)
>>> PowerSet(PowerSet(S.EmptySet))
PowerSet(PowerSet(EmptySet))
```

  Copy to clipboard

A power set of an infinite set:

```
>>> PowerSet(S.Reals)
PowerSet(Reals)
```

  Copy to clipboard

Evaluating the power set of a finite set to its explicit form:

```
>>> PowerSet(FiniteSet(1, 2, 3)).rewrite(FiniteSet)
FiniteSet(EmptySet, {1}, {2}, {3}, {1, 2}, {1, 3}, {2, 3}, {1, 2, 3})
```

  Copy to clipboard

Condition Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.conditionset)

# Condition Sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#module-sympy.sets.conditionset)

class sympy.sets.conditionset.ConditionSet(  *sym*, *condition*, *base_set=UniversalSet*,  )[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/conditionset.py#L20-L247)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.conditionset.ConditionSet)

Set of elements which satisfies a given condition.

   {𝑥∣condition⁡(𝑥)=𝚃𝚛𝚞𝚎,𝑥∈𝑆}

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Symbol, S, ConditionSet, pi, Eq, sin, Interval
>>> from sympy.abc import x, y, z
```

  Copy to clipboard

```
>>> sin_sols = ConditionSet(x, Eq(sin(x), 0), Interval(0, 2*pi))
>>> 2*pi in sin_sols
True
>>> pi/2 in sin_sols
False
>>> 3*pi in sin_sols
False
>>> 5 in ConditionSet(x, x**2 > 4, S.Reals)
True
```

  Copy to clipboard

If the value is not in the base set, the result is false:

```
>>> 5 in ConditionSet(x, x**2 > 4, Interval(2, 4))
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

Notes

Symbols with assumptions should be avoided or else the condition may evaluate without consideration of the set:

```
>>> n = Symbol('n', negative=True)
>>> cond = (n > 0); cond
False
>>> ConditionSet(n, cond, S.Integers)
EmptySet
```

  Copy to clipboard

Only free symbols can be changed by using 𝑠⁢𝑢⁢𝑏⁢𝑠:

```
>>> c = ConditionSet(x, x < 1, {x, z})
>>> c.subs(x, y)
ConditionSet(x, x < 1, {y, z})
```

  Copy to clipboard

To check if `pi` is in `c` use:

```
>>> pi in c
False
```

  Copy to clipboard

If no base set is specified, the universal set is implied:

```
>>> ConditionSet(x, x < 1).base_set
UniversalSet
```

  Copy to clipboard

Only symbols or symbol-like expressions can be used:

```
>>> ConditionSet(x + 1, x + 1 < 1, S.Integers)
Traceback (most recent call last):
...
ValueError: non-symbol dummy not recognized in condition
```

  Copy to clipboard

When the base set is a ConditionSet, the symbols will be unified if possible with preference for the outermost symbols:

```
>>> ConditionSet(x, x < y, ConditionSet(z, z + y < 2, S.Integers))
ConditionSet(x, (x < y) & (x + y < 2), Integers)
```

# SetKind[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#setkind)

class sympy.sets.conditionset.SetKind(*element_kind=None*)[[source]](https://github.com/sympy/sympy/blob/2d283a82d15f2b46beff7be5399546c79613c445/sympy/sets/sets.py#L2785-L2830)[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#sympy.sets.conditionset.SetKind)

SetKind is kind for all Sets

Every instance of Set will have kind `SetKind` parametrised by the kind of the elements of the `Set`. The kind of the elements might be `NumberKind`, or `TupleKind` or something else. When not all elements have the same kind then the kind of the elements will be given as `UndefinedKind`.

  Parameters:

**element_kind: Kind (optional)**

>
> The kind of the elements of the set. In a well defined set all elements
> will have the same kind. Otherwise the kind should
> sympy.core.kind.UndefinedKind. The element_kind argument is optional but
> should only be omitted in the case of EmptySet whose kind is simply
> SetKind()
>

Examples

```
>>> from sympy import Interval
>>> Interval(1, 2).kind
SetKind(NumberKind)
>>> Interval(1,2).kind.element_kind
NumberKind
```

  Copy to clipboard

See also

[`sympy.core.kind.NumberKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/core.html#sympy.core.kind.NumberKind), [`sympy.matrices.kind.MatrixKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/matrices/kind.html#sympy.matrices.kind.MatrixKind), [`sympy.core.containers.TupleKind`](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/core.html#sympy.core.containers.TupleKind)

Iteration over sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#iteration-over-sets)

# Iteration over sets[¶](https://docs.sympy.org/dev/modules/sets.html#iteration-over-sets)

For set unions, {𝑎,𝑏} ∪{𝑥,𝑦} can be treated as {𝑎,𝑏,𝑥,𝑦} for iteration regardless of the distinctiveness of the elements, however, for set intersections, assuming that {𝑎,𝑏} ∩{𝑥,𝑦} is ∅ or {𝑎,𝑏} would not always be valid, since some of 𝑎, 𝑏, 𝑥 or 𝑦 may or may not be the elements of the intersection.

Iterating over the elements of a set involving intersection, complement, or symmetric difference yields (possibly duplicate) elements of the set provided that all elements are known to be the elements of the set. If any element cannot be determined to be a member of a set then the iteration gives `TypeError`. This happens in the same cases where `x in y` would give an error.

There are some reasons to implement like this, even if it breaks the consistency with how the python set iterator works. We keep in mind that sympy set comprehension like `FiniteSet(*s)` from a existing sympy sets could be a common usage. And this approach would make `FiniteSet(*s)` to be consistent with any symbolic set processing methods like `FiniteSet(*simplify(s))`.

Integrity note

NDJSON records are canonical for this immutable Capsule. Tree, manifest display, and projection are generated views. Artifact records include SHA-256 hashes.
